claim: CaV1.3 channels regulate excitability in many neurons.
source: CaV1.3 channels regulate excitability in many neurons.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that is supported by the broader literature context and the experimental findings presented in the paper.

claim: Individual CaV1.3 channels are widely assumed to behave independently with respect to voltage-activation, open probability, and facilitation.
source: As is the case for all voltage-gated channels, it is widely assumed that individual CaV1.3 channels behave independently with respect to voltage-activation, open probability, and facilitation.
evidence: This statement reflects the prevailing assumption in the field that the authors are challenging.

claim: The short channel isoform (CaV1.3S), but not the long (CaV1.3L), associates in functional clusters of two or more channels that open cooperatively.
source: We found that the short channel isoform (CaV1.3S), but not the long (CaV1.3L), associates in functional clusters of two or more channels that open cooperatively, facilitating Ca2+ influx.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by multiple experimental approaches including super-resolution imaging, sparklet recordings, and coupling coefficient analysis.

claim: CaV1.3S channels are coupled via a C-terminus-to-C-terminus interaction.
source: CaV1.3S channels are coupled via a C-terminus-to-C-terminus interaction that requires binding of the incoming Ca2+ to calmodulin (CaM) and subsequent binding of CaM to the pre-IQ domain of the channels.
evidence: This mechanism is demonstrated through split Venus experiments, optogenetic dimerization, and mutagenesis studies.

claim: The coupling of CaV1.3S channels requires binding of incoming Ca2+ to calmodulin (CaM).
source: CaV1.3S channels are coupled via a C-terminus-to-C-terminus interaction that requires binding of the incoming Ca2+ to calmodulin (CaM) and subsequent binding of CaM to the pre-IQ domain of the channels.
evidence: This is supported by experiments using CaM inhibitory peptide (MLCKp) and dominant-negative CaM (CaM1234) that prevent channel coupling.

claim: The coupling of CaV1.3S channels requires subsequent binding of CaM to the pre-IQ domain of the channels.
source: CaV1.3S channels are coupled via a C-terminus-to-C-terminus interaction that requires binding of the incoming Ca2+ to calmodulin (CaM) and subsequent binding of CaM to the pre-IQ domain of the channels.
evidence: This is demonstrated by mutagenesis experiments showing that mutations in the pre-IQ domain (AAE mutant) prevent coupling, while mutations in the IQ domain (I1608E) do not.

claim: Physically-coupled CaV1.3S channels facilitate Ca2+ currents as a consequence of their higher open probabilities.
source: Physically-coupled channels facilitate Ca2+ currents as a consequence of their higher open probabilities, leading to increased firing rates in rat hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is supported by NPo analysis showing increased channel activity with Ca2+ as charge carrier, and sparklet recordings showing increased activity after depolarization-induced coupling.

claim: Cooperative gating of CaV1.3S channels leads to increased firing rates in rat hippocampal neurons.
source: Physically-coupled channels facilitate Ca2+ currents as a consequence of their higher open probabilities, leading to increased firing rates in rat hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is demonstrated by current-clamp recordings showing that optogenetically-induced coupling of CaV1.3S channels increases action potential firing rate by about 40%.

claim: CaV1.3 channels are widely expressed in neurons throughout the brain and spinal cord.
source: CaV1.3 channels are widely expressed in neurons throughout the brain and spinal cord (Tan et al., 2011), where they serve a number of critical functions including the modulation of resting potentials, the amplification of synaptic currents and the generation and shaping of repetitive firing (Guzman et al., 2009; Olson et al., 2005; Striessnig et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CaV1.3 channels serve critical functions including the modulation of resting potentials, the amplification of synaptic currents and the generation and shaping of repetitive firing.
source: CaV1.3 channels are widely expressed in neurons throughout the brain and spinal cord (Tan et al., 2011), where they serve a number of critical functions including the modulation of resting potentials, the amplification of synaptic currents and the generation and shaping of repetitive firing (Guzman et al., 2009; Olson et al., 2005; Striessnig et al., 2006).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CaV1.3 channels are dihydropyridine-sensitive L-type Ca2+ channels composed of a pore-forming CaV1.3α1 subunit and accessory β and α2-δ subunits.
source: These channels are dihydropyridine-sensitive L-type Ca2+ channels composed of a pore-forming CaV1.3α1 subunit and accessory β and α2-δ subunits.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the structure of CaV1.3 channels.

claim: The carboxy-terminus (C-terminus) of the α1D subunit contains an EF hand domain as well as pre-IQ and IQ domains to which calmodulin (CaM) binds.
source: The carboxy-terminus (C-terminus) of the α1D subunit is structurally complex, containing an EF hand domain as well as pre-IQ and IQ domains to which the Ca2+-binding protein calmodulin (CaM) binds (Ben-Johny and Yue, 2014).
evidence: This structural information is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Alternative splicing results in the expression of 'long' and 'short' CaV1.3 channel isoforms that differ in the length of the C-terminus.
source: Alternative splicing results in the expression of 'long' and 'short' CaV1.3 channel isoforms that differ in the length of the C-terminus (Singh et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The splice variant 42A (CaV1.3S) has a short C-terminus of 183 amino acids long compared to the 695 amino acids of the long isoform (CaV1.3L).
source: The splice variant 42A (CaV1.3S) has a short C-terminus of 183 amino acids long compared to the 695 amino acids of the long isoform (CaV1.3L).
evidence: This is factual information about the structural differences between the two isoforms.

claim: CaV1.3S channels lack the C-terminal modulatory domain (CTM), comprised of proximal (PCRD) and distal (DCRD) regulatory domains that block CaM binding to the IQ domain.
source: The CaV1.3S channels lack the so-called C-terminal modulatory domain (CTM), comprised of proximal (PCRD) and distal (DCRD) regulatory domains that block CaM binding to the IQ domain (Figures 1A and B, left).
evidence: This structural difference is illustrated in Figure 1A and B and is established knowledge about these isoforms.

claim: CaV1.3S channels activate at lower voltages than CaV1.3L channels.
source: As a consequence, CaV1.3S channels activate at lower voltages, have a higher open probability, and inactivate faster than CaV1.3L channels (Bock et al., 2011; Singh et al., 2008; Tan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CaV1.3S channels have a higher open probability than CaV1.3L channels.
source: As a consequence, CaV1.3S channels activate at lower voltages, have a higher open probability, and inactivate faster than CaV1.3L channels (Bock et al., 2011; Singh et al., 2008; Tan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CaV1.3S channels inactivate faster than CaV1.3L channels.
source: As a consequence, CaV1.3S channels activate at lower voltages, have a higher open probability, and inactivate faster than CaV1.3L channels (Bock et al., 2011; Singh et al., 2008; Tan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature and confirmed by the data in Figure 1.

claim: CaV1.3 channels carry about 20% of the L-type calcium current in hippocampal neurons.
source: CaV1.3 channels carry about 20% of the L-type calcium current in hippocampal neurons (Moosmang et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CaV1.3S channels are a good candidate for underlying the sustained neuronal firing and the persistent low-voltage-activated current observed in CA3 neurons.
source: As CaV1.3S channels activate at low voltages, they are a particular good candidate for underlying the sustained the neuronal firing and the persistent low- voltage-activated current observed in CA3 neurons (Avery and Johnston, 1996).
evidence: This is an inference based on the biophysical properties of CaV1.3S channels and previous observations in CA3 neurons.

claim: CaV1.3 channels support spontaneous firing of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra and mid-spiny striatal neurons.
source: In fact, CaV1.3 channels support spontaneous firing of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra and mid-spiny striatal neurons (Guzman et al., 2009; Olson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The function of CaV1.3 channels is tightly regulated by changes in intracellular Ca2+ ([Ca2+]i).
source: The function of CaV1.3 channels is tightly regulated by changes in intracellular Ca2+ ([Ca2+]i).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CaV1.3 channel regulation.

claim: The opening of CaV1.3 channels causes a local increase in [Ca2+]i that induces two opposing regulatory mechanisms: Ca2+-dependent inactivation (CDI) and Ca2+-dependent facilitation (CDF).
source: The opening of CaV1.3 channels causes a local increase in [Ca2+]i that induces two opposing regulatory mechanisms: Ca2+-dependent inactivation (CDI) and Ca2+-dependent facilitation (CDF) (Ben-Johny and Yue, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CDF manifests as an increase in the magnitude of the CaV1.3 current (ICa) with repetitive activation.
source: CDF manifests as an increase in the magnitude of the CaV1.3 current (ICa) with repetitive activation.
evidence: This is a definition of CDF based on established knowledge.

claim: In neurons, CDF can induce a persistent ICa that increases firing rate and may even lead to self-sustained firing.
source: In neurons, CDF can induce a persistent ICa that increases firing rate and may even lead to self-sustained firing (Fransen et al., 2006; Major and Tank, 2004; Sheffield et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: It has been proposed that CDF of the CaV1.3 channel depends on Ca2+/CaM-dependent kinase II (CaMKII)-mediated phosphorylation.
source: It has been proposed that CDF of the CaV1.3 channel depends on Ca2+/CaM-dependent kinase II (CaMKII)-mediated phosphorylation, as has also been proposed for the closely related CaV1.2 channel (Hudmon et al., 2005; Xiao et al., 1994; Yuan and Bers, 1994).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from previous literature, supported by citations.

claim: CaMKII-mediated phosphorylation requires the presence of a second protein, densin, which binds to the PDZ domain located in the most distal part of the C-terminus of the channel.
source: This phosphorylation requires the presence of a second protein, densin, which binds to the PDZ domain located in the most distal part of the C-terminus of the channel (Jenkins et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CaV1.3S lacks the PDZ domain, making CaMKII-mediated phosphorylation unlikely to be responsible for CDF in CaV1.3S channels.
source: Because CaV1.3S lacks that PDZ domain, CaMKII-mediated phosphorylation is unlikely to be responsible for CDF in CaV1.3S channels.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the structural differences between CaV1.3S and CaV1.3L.

claim: The mechanisms underlying the CDF of the widely expressed CaV1.3S channel have not yet been resolved.
source: Thus, the mechanisms underlying the CDF of the widely expressed CaV1.3S channel have not yet been resolved.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: Ca2+-induced interactions between the C-termini of neighboring CaV1.2 channels facilitates Ca2+ influx by increasing the activity of adjoined channels in cardiac muscle.
source: Two recent studies by Dixon et al. (Dixon et al., 2012; 2015) have suggested the tantalizing hypothesis that Ca2+-induced interactions between the C-termini of neighboring CaV1.2 channels facilitates Ca2+ influx by increasing the activity of adjoined channels in cardiac muscle.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous studies by Dixon et al.

claim: Whether physical and functional coupling of CaV1.2 channels is a common mechanism for the control of Ca2+ influx via voltage-gated Ca2+ channel function, including CaV1.3 channels, is unknown.
source: At present, however, whether this physical and functional coupling of CaV1.2 channels is a common mechanism for the control of Ca2+ influx via voltage-gated Ca2+ channel function, including CaV1.3 channels is unknown.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: The possibility that cooperative CaV1.3 channel gating regulates neuronal excitability is unclear.
source: Furthermore, the possibility that cooperative CaV1.3 channel gating regulates neuronal excitability is also unclear.
evidence: This statement identifies a gap in knowledge that the current study addresses.

claim: CaV1.3S channels form functional clusters of two or more channels along the surface membrane of hippocampal neurons.
source: In the present study, using electrophysiological, optogenetic, and super-resolution imaging approaches, we discovered that CaV1.3S channels form functional clusters of two or more channels along the surface membrane of hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by super-resolution imaging and photobleaching experiments.

claim: Clustered CaV1.3S channels undergo Ca2+-induced physical interactions that increase the activity of adjoined channels.
source: Clustered CaV1.3S channels undergo Ca2+-induced physical interactions that increase the activity of adjoined channels, facilitate Ca2+ currents and thereby increase firing rates in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is a primary finding supported by split Venus experiments, sparklet recordings, and electrophysiology.

claim: Cooperative gating of CaV1.3S channels is a new general mechanism for the amplification of Ca2+ signals in excitable cells.
source: We propose that cooperative gating of CaV1.3S channels is a new general mechanism for the amplification of Ca2+ signals in excitable cells.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings presented in the study.

claim: Membrane depolarization induced large CaV1.3L currents that inactivated slowly with Ba2+ in the external solution.
source: With Ba2+ in the external solution, membrane depolarization induced large CaV1.3L currents that inactivated slowly (Figure 1A, center).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: Switching to a perfusion solution containing Ca2+ decreased the amplitude of CaV1.3L currents by nearly 40% and increased the rate of inactivation.
source: Switching to a perfusion solution containing Ca2+ decreased the amplitude of CaV1.3L currents by nearly 40% and increased the rate of inactivation.
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1A.

claim: The difference in the magnitude of CDI between CaV1.3S and CaV1.3L has been attributed to the lack of the CTM domain in CaV1.3S channels.
source: As discussed above, this difference in the magnitude of CDI has been attributed to the lack of the CTM domain in CaV1.3S channels.
evidence: This is an interpretation based on established knowledge about the structural differences between the isoforms.

claim: The amplitude of CaV1.3S currents decreased by only about 15% at -10 mV upon changing the external solution from Ba2+ to Ca2+.
source: Curiously, the amplitude of CaV1.3S currents decreased to a lesser extent (only about 15% at -10 mV) upon changing the external solution from Ba2+ to Ca2+ (Figure 1B, center).
evidence: This is directly observed in the experimental data shown in Figure 1B.

claim: At -30 mV, the amplitudes of elementary CaV1.3S and CaV1.3L channel currents with Ca2+ as the charge carrier were -0.48 ± 0.07 and -0.49 ± 0.01 pA, respectively.
source: For example, at -30 mV they were -0.48 ± 0.07 and -0.49 ± 0.01 pA for CaV1.3L and CaV1.3S channels, respectively (Figures 1C–F).
evidence: This is directly measured from single channel recordings shown in Figures 1C-F.

claim: The unitary current values at -30 mV are in accordance with the unitary currents reported by Guia et al. for cardiac L-type channels using Ca2+ as charge carrier.
source: These values are in accordance with the unitary currents reported by Guia et al. for cardiac L-type channels using Ca2+ as charge carrier (Guia et al., 2001).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous literature to validate the measurements.

claim: The single channel currents produced during the opening of CaV1.3L and CaV1.3S channels were both larger with Ba2+ as the charge carrier than with Ca2+.
source: Furthermore, as is the case for other CaV1 channels, the single channel currents produced during the opening of CaV1.3L and CaV1.3S channels were both larger with Ba2+ as the charge carrier than with Ca2+ (-1.14 ± 0.02 pA and -1.10 ± 0.02 pA for CaV1.3L and CaV1.3S at -30 mV, respectively), but not significantly different from each other (Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is directly measured from single channel recordings shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: The amplitude of the unitary currents with Ba2+ is in accordance with previously reported values for these channels.
source: The amplitude of the unitary currents with Ba2+ is also in accordance with previously reported values for these channels (Bock et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous literature to validate the measurements.

claim: The difference observed in the macroscopic currents between the CaV1.3L and CaV1.3S channels is not due to differences in unitary currents.
source: These data suggest that the difference observed in the macroscopic currents between the CaV1.3L and CaV1.3S channels is not due to differences in unitary currents.
evidence: This is an inference based on the finding that unitary currents are similar between the two isoforms.

claim: Ca2+ enhances the activation of CaV1.3S, but not CaV1.3L channels by increasing the channel activity (NPo).
source: We then tested the hypothesis that Ca2+ enhances the activation of CaV1.3S, but not CaV1.3L channels by increasing the channel activity (NPo).
evidence: This hypothesis is tested and supported by the NPo analysis shown in Figures 1I and J.

claim: For ICa to be similar to IBa in CaV1.3S channels, the NPo of CaV1.3S must be higher in the presence of Ca2+ than Ba2+.
source: Since elementary CaV1.3L and CaV1.3S currents are larger when Ba2+ rather than Ca2+ is the charge carrier, for ICa to be similar to IBa, the NPo of CaV1.3S must be higher in the presence of Ca2+ than Ba2+.
evidence: This is a logical inference based on the relationship between whole-cell current, unitary current, and NPo.

claim: There was no significant difference in the activation time constants for CaV1.3L and CaV1.3S currents (1.60 ± 0.22 and 1.17 ± 0.051 ms at -10 mV, respectively, p = 0.112).
source: This assumption is reasonable, as we found no significant difference in the activation time constants for CaV1.3L and CaV1.3S currents that were 1.60 ± 0.22 and 1.17 ± 0.051 ms (-10 mV, n = 6 for each channel, p = 0.112), respectively.
evidence: This is directly measured from the experimental data.

claim: Ca2+ ions entering the cell through the channels increased the NPo nearly 1.5-fold for CaV1.3S channels, but not at all for CaV1.3L channels.
source: We found that Ca2+ ions entering the cell through the channels increased the NPo nearly 1.5-fold for CaV1.3S channels, but not at all for CaV1.3L channels (Figures 1I and J).
evidence: This is directly calculated from the experimental data shown in Figures 1I and J.

claim: A Ca2+-dependent mechanism enhances inward Ca2+ currents by increasing the Po of CaV1.3S channels, but not that of CaV1.3L channels.
source: Thus, assuming that the number of functional CaV1.3 channels (N) in the membrane remained constant, a reasonable assumption given the short time lapse (~2 min) between recording IBa and ICa from the same cell, these data suggest that a Ca2+-dependent mechanism enhances inward Ca2+ currents by increasing the Po of CaV1.3S channels, but not that of CaV1.3L channels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the NPo analysis and the assumption that N remains constant.

claim: One possible explanation for the Ca2+-influx–dependent increase in the Po of CaV1.3S channels is cooperative gating among channels in small clusters.
source: One possible explanation for the Ca2+-influx–dependent increase in the Po of CaV1.3S channels is cooperative gating among channels in small clusters, as we have previously reported for CaV1.2 channels in cardiomyocytes and smooth muscle cells (Navedo et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a hypothesis proposed by the authors based on their previous work with CaV1.2 channels.

claim: CaV1.3S sparklets were recorded at a membrane potential of -80 mV in the presence of 20 mM external Ca2+.
source: CaV1.3S sparklets were recorded at a membrane potential of -80 mV in the presence of 20 mM external Ca2+; 10 mM EGTA was included in the patch pipette to confine the [Ca2+]i signal to within ~1 µm of the point of Ca2+ entry (Zenisek et al., 2003).
evidence: This describes the experimental conditions for sparklet recordings.

claim: A quantal analysis of CaV1.3S and CaV1.3L sparklets revealed the presence of single-level (elementary) events with a mean amplitude of ~40 nM for both channels.
source: A quantal analysis of CaV1.3S and CaV1.3L sparklets revealed the presence of single-level (elementary) events with a mean amplitude of ~40 nM for both channels, in agreement with our previous study (Navedo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is directly measured from sparklet recordings and is consistent with previous work.

claim: Multi-quantal sparklets were more commonly observed in cells expressing CaV1.3S than CaV1.3L channels.
source: Interestingly, consistent with our single channel data, we found that multi-quantal sparklets, which presumably result from the simultaneous opening of several CaV1.3 channels, were more commonly observed in cells expressing CaV1.3S than CaV1.3L channels (Figure 2A).
evidence: This is directly observed in the sparklet recordings shown in Figure 2A.

claim: The average coupling coefficient (κ) value for CaV1.3S and CaV1.3L channels was 0.21 ± 0.05 (n = 15) and 0.08 ± 0.04 (n = 12), respectively.
source: Using this approach, we found that the average κ value for CaV1.3S and CaV1.3L channels was 0.21 ± 0.05 (n = 15) and 0.08 ± 0.04 (n = 12), respectively (Figure 2B).
evidence: This is directly calculated from sparklet recordings using a coupled Markov-chain model, as shown in Figure 2B.

claim: CaV1.3S channels are more likely to undergo cooperative gating, generating persistent and greater Ca2+ influx than CaV1.3L channels.
source: These results support the hypothesis that CaV1.3S channels are more likely to undergo cooperative gating, generating persistent and greater Ca2+ influx than CaV1.3L channels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the coupling coefficient analysis.

claim: CaV1.3 channels form clusters occupying an average area of 3660 ± 80 nm2 (n = 5) in hippocampal neurons.
source: This analysis showed that CaV1.3 channels form clusters occupying an average area of 3660 ± 80 nm2 (n = 5).
evidence: This is directly measured from super-resolution imaging of hippocampal neurons.

claim: The antibody used in this study has been shown to not recognize the corresponding sequence of the closely related CaV1.2 α subunit in both transfected cells and hippocampal tissue.
source: The antibody used in this study has been shown to not recognize the corresponding sequence of the closely related CaV1.2 α subunit in both, transfected cells and hippocampal tissue (Hell et al., 1993; 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature validating the antibody specificity.

claim: CaV1.3L and CaV1.3S channels form clusters of similar size along the surface membrane in tsA-201 cells.
source: Super-resolution imaging shows that CaV1.3L and CaV1.3S channels form clusters of similar size along the surface membrane, but CaV1.3L channels, unlike CaV1.3S channels, do not undergo physical and functional coupling.
evidence: This is directly observed in super-resolution imaging shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The mean areas of CaV1.3L and CaV1.3S channel clusters were 2543 ± 50 nm2 and 2119 ± 73 nm2, respectively (n = 7) in tsA-201 cells.
source: The mean areas of CaV1.3L and CaV1.3S channel clusters were 2543 ± 50 nm2 and 2119 ± 73 nm2, respectively (Figure 3—figure supplement 1G, n = 7).
evidence: This is directly measured from super-resolution imaging shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1G.

claim: The majority (65%) of CaV1.3S clusters underwent at least five stepwise decreases in fluorescence during photobleaching.
source: The majority (65%) of CaV1.3S clusters underwent at least five stepwise decreases in fluorescence, with the remaining clusters showing fewer steps.
evidence: This is directly observed in photobleaching experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: A single photobleaching step was observed in only 4% of the CaV1.3S clusters.
source: A single photobleaching step was observed in only 4% of the CaV1.3S clusters.
evidence: This is directly observed in photobleaching experiments shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The mean number of CaV1.3S channels per cluster determined through sequential photobleaching was 8 ± 1 (n = 1105 clusters, 18 cells) in hippocampal neurons.
source: The mean number of CaV1.3S channels per cluster determined through sequential photobleaching was 8 ± 1 (n = 1105 clusters, 18 cells) in hippocampal neurons, this number is consistent with the average cluster area calculated from our super-resolution data and is similar to that reported in two different studies on the L-type channel distribution in hippocampal neurons using immunogold-labeling with electron microscopy and high-resolution immunofluorescence techniques (Leitch et al., 2009; Obermair et al., 2004).
evidence: This is directly measured from photobleaching experiments and is consistent with previous literature.

claim: Step-photobleaching in tsA-201 cells revealed an average of 5 ± 1 CaV1.3S channels per cluster (n = 585 clusters, 11 cells).
source: Step-photobleaching in tsA-201 cells revealed an average of 5 ± 1 CaV1.3S channels per cluster (n = 585 clusters, 11 cells), consistent also with our super-resolution cluster area measurements (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is directly measured from photobleaching experiments shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Multi-quantal events detected by imaging Ca2+ influx represent the simultaneous activity of multiple CaV1.3S channels in a membrane microdomain.
source: Collectively, these results support our working hypothesis that multi-quantal events detected by imaging Ca2+ influx represent the simultaneous activity of multiple CaV1.3S channels in a membrane microdomain.
evidence: This is an inference based on the clustering and photobleaching data.

claim: In cells expressing CaV1.3S-CIBN and CaV1.3S-CRY2 channels, ICa amplitude increased by 35% (n = 6, p<0.001) after blue light illumination.
source: As shown in Figure 4C, in cells expressing CaV1.3S-CIBN and CaV1.3S-CRY2 channels, ICa amplitude increased by 35% (n = 6, p<0.001) after illumination, whereas in cells expressing CaV1.3L-CIBN and CaV1.3L-CRY2 channels, there was no change in current amplitude (0.95 ± 0.03 n = 6).
evidence: This is directly measured from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: In cells expressing CaV1.3L-CIBN and CaV1.3L-CRY2 channels, there was no change in current amplitude after blue light illumination (0.95 ± 0.03 n = 6).
source: As shown in Figure 4C, in cells expressing CaV1.3S-CIBN and CaV1.3S-CRY2 channels, ICa amplitude increased by 35% (n = 6, p<0.001) after illumination, whereas in cells expressing CaV1.3L-CIBN and CaV1.3L-CRY2 channels, there was no change in current amplitude (0.95 ± 0.03 n = 6).
evidence: This is directly measured from optogenetic experiments shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Fusing adjacent channels at the tip of their C-tail increases the probability of functional coupling between CaV1.3S adjoined channels but not between CaV1.3L channels.
source: These results suggest that fusing adjacent channels at the tip of their C-tail increase the probability of functional coupling between CaV1.3S adjoined channels but not between CaV1.3L channels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the optogenetic dimerization experiments.

claim: The normalized conductance and Venus fluorescence exhibited similar sigmoidal voltage dependencies for CaV1.3S channels in 20 mM Ca2+.
source: The normalized conductance and Venus fluorescence exhibited similar sigmoidal voltage dependencies (Figures 5C–D), which can be attributed to the irreversible nature of the Venus reconstitution, resulting in an increased number of fluorescent proteins with each successive depolarization as the open probability of CaV1.3S channels increases.
evidence: This is directly observed in the split Venus experiments shown in Figures 5C-D.

claim: Substituting 2 mM Ba2+ for 20 mM Ca2+ in the external solution led to a robust IBa during membrane depolarization, but caused no accompanying change in Venus fluorescence.
source: Substituting 2 mM Ba2+ for 20 mM Ca2+ in the external solution led to a robust IBa during membrane depolarization, but caused no accompanying change in Venus fluorescence (Figures 5F–I).
evidence: This is directly observed in the split Venus experiments shown in Figures 5F-I.

claim: Venus reconstitution was never observed in cells expressing CaV1.3L-VN and CaV1.3L-VC.
source: Importantly, Venus reconstitution was never observed in cells expressing CaV1.3L-VN and CaV1.3L-VC in (see Figure 8).
evidence: This is directly observed in the split Venus experiments shown in Figure 8.

claim: CaV1.3S channels can physically interact via their C-termini in response to membrane depolarization, and this association is promoted by intracellular Ca2+.
source: These data indicate that CaV1.3S channels, but not CaV1.3L channels, can physically interact via their C-termini, that this association occurs in response to membrane depolarization, and that it is promoted by intracellular Ca2+.
evidence: This is an inference based on the split Venus experiments showing Ca2+-dependent but not Ba2+-dependent Venus reconstitution.

claim: Ca2+-induced fusion of CaV1.3S-VN and CaV1.3S-VC increases the activity of adjoined channels.
source: Thus, we tested the hypothesis that Ca2+-induced fusion of CaV1.3S-VN and CaV1.3S-VC increases the activity of adjoined channels by recording CaV1.3S sparklets at a holding potential of -80 mV, in the presence of Ba2+ or Ca2+, before and after applying the same depolarization protocol described above.
evidence: This hypothesis is tested and supported by sparklet recordings shown in Figure 5J-M.

claim: After depolarization, CaV1.3S sparklet activity (nPs) and sparklet density markedly increased in the presence of Ca2+, but not Ba2+.
source: Before depolarization, CaV1.3S sparklet activity was very low (Figure 5J); after depolarization, CaV1.3S sparklet activity (nPs; Figure 5K) and sparklet density (Figure 5L) markedly increased in the presence of Ca2+, but not Ba2+, without a change in the amplitude of the elementary Ca2+ influx (Figure 5M).
evidence: This is directly observed in sparklet recordings shown in Figures 5J-M.

claim: Dialysis of MLCKp or co-expression of CaM1234 prevented CaV1.3S-VN and CaV1.3S-VC fusion upon membrane depolarization.
source: Dialysis of MLCKp or co-expression of CaM1234 prevented CaV1.3S-VN and CaV1.3S-VC fusion upon membrane depolarization (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: This is directly observed in the split Venus experiments shown in Figures 6A-D.

claim: The fraction of peak ICa remaining at 300 ms (r300) in MLCKp-dialyzed cells (0.11 ± 0.03, n = 5) was similar to that of controls (0.14 ± 0.03, n = 5).
source: Whereas the fraction of peak ICa remaining at 300 ms (r300) in MLCKp-dialyzed cells (0.11 ± 0.03, n = 5) was similar to that of controls (0.14 ± 0.03, n = 5), the rate of inactivation of ICa was slower in cells expressing CaM1234, as reflected in a much higher r300 value (0.75 ± 0.05, n = 5) (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is directly measured from electrophysiology experiments shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The rate of inactivation of ICa was slower in cells expressing CaM1234, as reflected in a much higher r300 value (0.75 ± 0.05, n = 5).
source: Whereas the fraction of peak ICa remaining at 300 ms (r300) in MLCKp-dialyzed cells (0.11 ± 0.03, n = 5) was similar to that of controls (0.14 ± 0.03, n = 5), the rate of inactivation of ICa was slower in cells expressing CaM1234, as reflected in a much higher r300 value (0.75 ± 0.05, n = 5) (Figure 6F).
evidence: This is directly measured from electrophysiology experiments shown in Figure 6F.

claim: The CaM molecules involved in CDI are distinct from those involved in functional coupling of CaV1.3S channels.
source: Our interpretation of these findings is that the CaM molecules involved in CDI are distinct from those involved in functional coupling of CaV1.3S channels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential effects of MLCKp and CaM1234 on CDI versus channel coupling.

claim: The coupling coefficient for CaV1.3S sparklet sites in WT cells was 0.07 ± 0.06, whereas that in CaM1234 cells was 0.02 ± 0.02 (n = 5).
source: The coupling coefficient for CaV1.3S sparklet sites in WT cells was 0.07 ± 06, whereas that in CaM1234 cells was 0.02 ± 0.02 (n = 5).
evidence: This is directly calculated from sparklet recordings.

claim: Membrane depolarization increased the coupling coefficient of CaV1.3S channels within multi-quantal sparklet sites in control cells (0.18 ± 0.03, n = 5), but not in CaM1234 cells (0.08 ± 0.05, n = 5).
source: Membrane depolarization increased the coupling coefficient of CaV1.3S channels within multi-quantal sparklet sites in control cells (0.18 ± 0.03, n = 5), but not in CaM1234 cells (0.08 ± 0.05, n = 5).
evidence: This is directly calculated from sparklet recordings.

claim: Depolarization increased CaV1.3 sparklet activity nearly 7-fold in control cells, but had no effect on sparklet activity in CaM1234 cells.
source: However, depolarization increased CaV1.3 sparklet activity nearly 7-fold in control cells, but had no effect on sparklet activity in CaM1234 cells.
evidence: This is directly measured from sparklet recordings shown in Figure 6I.

claim: Ca2+ binding to CaM is required for physical and functional CaV1.3S-to-CaV1.3S channel coupling.
source: Taken together with the ICa and Venus reconstitution results described above, these data strongly suggest that Ca2+ binding to CaM is required for physical and functional CaV1.3S-to-CaV1.3S channel coupling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the experiments with CaM1234 and MLCKp.

claim: CaV1.3-I1608E channels showed a slower rate of inactivation than control and CaV1.3S-AAE channels.
source: CaV1.3S-I1608E channels showed a slower rate of inactivation than control and CaV1.3S-AAE channels (Figure 7B), consistent with the lack of CDI.
evidence: This is directly observed in electrophysiology experiments shown in Figure 7B.

claim: CaV1.3S-I1608E-VN/VC, but not CaV1.3S-AAE VN/VC, were capable of reconstituting Venus during membrane depolarization.
source: Interestingly, CaV1.3S-I1608E-VN/VC, but not CaV1.3S-AAE VN/VC, which were capable of reconstituting Venus during membrane depolarization (Figure 7C–G).
evidence: This is directly observed in split Venus experiments shown in Figures 7C-G.

claim: Binding of CaM to the pre-IQ domain is critically involved in CaV1.3S channel coupling during membrane depolarization.
source: These data suggest that binding of CaM to the pre-IQ domain is critically involved in CaV1.3S channel coupling during membrane depolarization and further supports our previous assertion that the CaM pool involved in CDI is distinct from that involved in channel coupling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the mutagenesis experiments showing that pre-IQ mutations prevent coupling while IQ mutations do not.

claim: CDI of ICa was faster in cells expressing the CaV1.3L∆116 channels compared to the full length CaV1.3L channels (p<0.05).
source: As expected, CDI of ICa was faster in cells expressing the CaV1.3L∆116 channels compared to the full length CaV1.3L channels (p<0.05; Figure 8B and C).
evidence: This is directly observed in electrophysiology experiments shown in Figures 8B and C.

claim: Cells expressing CaV1.3L∆116 channels failed to reconstitute Venus fluorescence with 2 mM Ca2+ in the bathing solution.
source: We found that, with 2 mM Ca2+ in the bathing solution, cells expressing CaV1.3L∆116 channels failed to reconstitute Venus fluorescence, similar to what we observed for the full length CaV1.3L channel (Figure 8D–G).
evidence: This is directly observed in split Venus experiments shown in Figures 8D-G.

claim: Even increasing the extracellular Ca2+ concentration to 20 mM was not enough to induce coupling in the CaV1.3L∆116 channels.
source: Even increasing the extracellular Ca2+ concentration to 20 mM was not enough to induce coupling in the CaV1.3L∆116 channels (Figure 8—figure supplement 1, n = 5, p=0.245 -60 mV vs 20 mV).
evidence: This is directly observed in split Venus experiments shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1.

claim: Deletion of DCRD is not sufficient to allow coupling of CaV1.3L channels.
source: This result suggests that deletion of DCRD is not sufficient to allow coupling of CaV1.3L channels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the failure of CaV1.3L∆116 channels to undergo coupling.

claim: Ca2+ sparklets in hippocampal neurons were restricted to specific sites and had multi-quantal amplitudes resulting from the simultaneous opening and closing of multiple channels.
source: As in tsA-201 cells expressing CaV1.3S channels, Ca2+ sparklets in neurons were restricted to specific sites and had multi-quantal amplitudes resulting from the simultaneous opening and closing of multiple channels.
evidence: This is directly observed in sparklet recordings from hippocampal neurons.

claim: The quantal unit of Ca2+ influx in hippocampal neurons was about 40 nM.
source: The quantal unit of Ca2+ influx was about 40 nM.
evidence: This is directly measured from sparklet recordings in hippocampal neurons.

claim: The coupling coefficient (κ) of sparklet sites in hippocampal neurons ranged from 0.14 to 0.33, with an average κ value of 0.23 ± 0.04 (n = 6).
source: The coupling coefficient (κ) of sparklet sites ranged from 0.14 to 0.33. The average κ value was 0.23 ± 0.04 (n = 6).
evidence: This is directly calculated from sparklet recordings in hippocampal neurons.

claim: Sparklet site activity in hippocampal neurons was decreased by application of 300 nM of the dihydropyridine antagonist isradipine and completely eliminated when the concentration of the drug was increased to 10 µM.
source: Importantly, sparklet site activity was decreased by application of 300 nM of the dihydropyridine antagonist isradipine and completely eliminated when the concentration of the drug was increased to 10 µM (Figure 9A and B).
evidence: This is directly observed in sparklet recordings shown in Figures 9A and B.

claim: Sparklets in hippocampal neurons were produced by L-type calcium channels.
source: This is consistent with the hypothesis that sparklets in hippocampal neurons were produced by L-type calcium channels.
evidence: This is an inference based on the sensitivity of sparklets to dihydropyridine antagonists.

claim: CaV1.3 channels have a reduced sensitivity to dihydropyridines compared to CaV1.2 channels.
source: Both CaV1.2 and CaV1.3 channels are expressed in hippocampal neurons (Hell et al., 1993) and although it is impossible to distinguish between these two L-type Ca2+ channels using either electrophysiological or pharmacological methods, it has been shown that CaV1.3 channels have a reduced sensitivity to dihydropyridines compared to CaV1.2 channels (Lipscombe et al., 2004; Xu and Lipscombe, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: 100% of CaV1.2 channels but only ~60% of CaV1.3 channels are inhibited by 300 nM isradipine.
source: A previous study by Koschak et al found that 100% of CaV1.2 channels but only ~60% of CaV1.3 channels are inhibited by 300 nM isradipine (Koschak et al., 2001), given this, it is reasonable to assume that any sparklet remaining after application of 300 nM isradipine is more likely to be generated by CaV1.3channels than CaV1.2.
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Near by 25% of the L-type current in hippocampal neurons is carried by CaV1.3 channels.
source: In addition, near by 25% of the L-type current in hippocampal neurons is carried by CaV1.3 channels (Moosmang et al., 2005), this proportion is in agreement with the remaining sparklet site density we observed after the treatment with 300 nM isradipine (Figure 9C).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature and is consistent with the experimental observations.

claim: Conditioning membrane depolarization to 0 mV increased sparklet activity nearly 3-fold in hippocampal neurons and induced persistent sparklet activity.
source: As was the case for tsA-201 cells expressing CaV1.3S channels, we found that conditioning membrane depolarization to 0 mV increased sparklet activity nearly 3-fold in the hippocampal neurons and induced persistent sparklet activity (Figure 9D and E).
evidence: This is directly observed in sparklet recordings shown in Figures 9D and E.

claim: The coupling coefficient in hippocampal neurons increased from 0.15 ± 0.04 to 0.43 ± 0.12 after membrane depolarization (n = 8).
source: The coupling coefficient increased from 0.15 ± 0.04 to 0.43 ± 0.12 after membrane depolarization (n = 8).
evidence: This is directly calculated from sparklet recordings in hippocampal neurons.

claim: L-type channels undergo cooperative gating, generating persistent Ca2+ influx in hippocampal neurons.
source: These results support the hypothesis that L-type channels undergo cooperative gating, generating persistent Ca2+ influx in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the increased coupling coefficient and sparklet activity after depolarization.

claim: The persistent L-type channels sparklet activity evoked by membrane depolarization in the presence of Ca2+ bears a striking resemblance to the persistent cationic currents observed in several types of neurons.
source: The persistent L-type channels sparklet activity evoked by membrane depolarization in the presence of Ca2+ bears a striking resemblance to the persistent cationic currents observed in several types of neurons (Fransen et al., 2006; Major and Tank, 2004; Moritz et al., 2007; Powers and Binder, 2001).
evidence: This is a comparison to previous literature suggesting a potential physiological relevance.

claim: The somatic and dendritic membranes of neurons expressing both CaV1.3S-VN and CaV1.3S-VC channels displayed prominent Venus fluorescence.
source: We found that the somatic and dendritic membranes of neurons expressing both CaV1.3S-VN and CaV1.3S-VC channels displayed prominent Venus fluorescence (Figure 10A), indicating fusion of CaV1.3S-VN and CaV1.3S-VC channel pairs and functional Venus reconstitution.
evidence: This is directly observed in confocal imaging shown in Figure 10A.

claim: The C-termini of CaV1.3S channels make contact during normal neuronal firing.
source: Since Venus reconstitution is irreversible and neurons have spontaneous electrical activity, this observation suggests that the C-termini of CaV1.3S channels make contact during normal neuronal firing.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of Venus fluorescence in neurons with spontaneous activity.

claim: Expression of CaV1.3S-VN and CaV1.3S-VC channels increased the number of CaV1.3 channel clusters in hippocampal neurons, but not the size of the clusters.
source: We analyzed super resolution images of hippocampal neurons transfected with CaV1.3S-VN and CaV1.3S-VC and found that expression of these channels increased the number of CaV1.3 channel clusters in the cells, but not the size of the clusters (Figure 10—figure supplemental 1).
evidence: This is directly observed in super-resolution imaging shown in Figure 10—figure supplemental 1.

claim: The spontaneous fusion of CaV1.3S channels was not a consequence of their being over-expressed in the plasma membranes of the hippocampal neurons.
source: These results indicate that the spontaneous fusion of CaV1.3S channels was not a consequence of their being over-expressed in the plasma membranes of the hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that cluster size did not change with overexpression.

claim: Forced coupling of CaV1.3S-CIBN and CaV1.3S-CRY2 channel pairs increased the average firing rate by about 40% (p<0.01) in hippocampal neurons.
source: Forced coupling of CaV1.3S-CIBN and CaV1.3S-CRY2 channel pairs increased the average firing rate by about 40% (p<0.01, Figure 10C).
evidence: This is directly measured from current-clamp recordings shown in Figure 10C.

claim: 488 nm illumination produced no effect on firing rate in control hippocampal neurons transfected only with CaV1.3S-CIBN channels (0.90 ± 0.04, N = 4).
source: 488 nm illumination produced no effect on firing rate in control hippocampal neurons transfected only with CaV1.3S-CIBN channels (0.90 ± 0.04, N = 4).
evidence: This is a control experiment showing that light alone does not affect firing rate.

claim: Adding the L-type calcium channel blocker nifedipine 10 μM to the bathing solution abolished all AP activity after light-induced fusion of CaV1.3S-CIBN and CaV1.3S-CRY2.
source: Adding the L-type calcium channel blocker nifedipine 10 μM to the bathing solution abolished all AP activity after light-induced fusion of CaV1.3S-CIBN and CaV1.3S-CRY2 (Figure 10B, left trace and 10C).
evidence: This is directly observed in current-clamp recordings shown in Figures 10B and 10C.

claim: CaV1.3S channels play a crucial role in regulating the action potential firing in hippocampal neurons.
source: Together, these results highlight the crucial role that CaV1.3S channels play in regulating the action potential firing in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effects of forced coupling and nifedipine on neuronal firing.

claim: CaV1.3 channels in the plasma membrane of hippocampal neurons are arranged in clusters containing multiple (~8) channels.
source: We have found that CaV1.3 channels in the plasma membrane of hippocampal neurons are arranged in clusters containing multiple (~8) channels.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from super-resolution imaging and photobleaching experiments.

claim: Functional coupling of CaV1.3S channels is promoted by intracellular Ca2+ and involves physical interactions via channel C-termini mediated by physical interactions between Ca2+-CaM and the pre-IQ domain.
source: Functional coupling of CaV1.3S channels is promoted by intracellular Ca2+ and involves physical interactions via channel C-termini mediated by physical interactions between Ca2+-CaM and the pre-IQ domain.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from split Venus, mutagenesis, and CaM inhibition experiments.

claim: Ca2+-driven CaV1.3S channel coupling constitutes a novel feed-forward mechanism for the activation of these channels during membrane depolarization.
source: We propose that Ca2+-driven CaV1.3S channel coupling constitutes a novel feed-forward mechanism for the activation of these channels during membrane depolarization and provides an apparatus for Ca2+-dependent facilitation of inward L-type Ca2+ currents.
evidence: This is a proposed mechanism based on the experimental findings.

claim: These findings challenge a fundamental tenet of the classic Hodgkin-Huxley model of ion channel gating: that voltage-gated channels open and close independently.
source: Further, these findings challenge a fundamental tenet of the classic Hodgkin-Huxley model of ion channel gating: that voltage-gated channels open and close independently.
evidence: This is a broader implication of the findings regarding cooperative gating.

claim: CaV1.3S channel coupling is critically dependent on intracellular Ca2+ and CaM.
source: Our data suggest that CaV1.3S channel coupling is critically dependent on intracellular Ca2+ and CaM.
evidence: This is a summary of the findings from experiments with CaM inhibitors and mutants.

claim: During membrane depolarization, CaV1.3S channels open and Ca2+ flowing through these channels creates a local increase in [Ca2+]i near the mouth and C-terminus of the channel where CaM resides.
source: During membrane depolarization, CaV1.3S channels open. Ca2+ flowing through these channels creates a local increase in [Ca2+]i — a CaV1.3 sparklet — near the mouth and C-terminus of the channel where the Ca2+-binding protein CaM resides.
evidence: This is a mechanistic description based on the experimental findings.

claim: Upon binding Ca2+, CaM associates with the pre-IQ domain of the channels, enabling the formation of CaV1.3S-CaV1.3S 'couplets'.
source: Upon binding Ca2+, CaM associates with the pre-IQ domain of the channels, enabling the formation of CaV1.3S-CaV1.3S 'couplets'.
evidence: This is a mechanistic description based on the experimental findings with split Venus and mutagenesis.

claim: The observation of pre-IQ dimers of the structurally similar CaV1.2 channel undergoing coiled-coil interactions in vitro gives credence to this model.
source: The observation of pre-IQ dimers of the structurally similar CaV1.2 channel undergoing coiled-coil interactions in vitro (Fallon et al., 2009) and functionally couples to neighboring channels (Dixon et al., 2015) gives credence to this model.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature on CaV1.2 channels.

claim: Soluble as well as apo-CaM pre-associated with the channel could be involved in inducing physical channel-to-channel interactions.
source: The observation that CaM1234 and MLCKp prevent CaV1.3S coupling would suggest that soluble as well as apo-CaM pre-associated with the channel could be involved in inducing physical channel-to-channel interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the effects of CaM inhibitors and mutants.

claim: Because physically coupled CaV1.3S channels exhibit higher open probabilities, the overall activity of CaV1.3S channels within a cluster would depend on the number of channels forming dimers or the probability of the formation of higher order oligomers.
source: Because physically coupled CaV1.3S channels exhibit higher open probabilities, the overall activity of CaV1.3S channels within a cluster would then depend on the number of channels forming dimers or the probability of the formation of higher order oligomers.
evidence: This is an inference based on the relationship between coupling and channel activity.

claim: Minor and colleagues reported the formation of symmetric dimers of pre-IQ domains bridged by two CaM molecules.
source: It is important to note that Minor and colleagues reported the formation of symmetric dimers of pre-IQ domains bridged by two CaM molecules (Kim et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Minor and colleagues failed to obtain any clustering when CaV1.2 channels were expressed in Xenopus oocytes.
source: However, they failed to obtain any clustering when the channels were expressed in Xenopus oocytes.
evidence: This is a statement about previous findings in the literature.

claim: Clustering and functional coupling may be features of CaV1 channels expressed only in mammalian cells.
source: The cause for this apparent lack of clustering of CaV1.2 channels in the frog egg are unclear, but suggest that clustering and functional coupling may be features of CaV1 channels expressed only in mammalian cells, as we have shown here for CaV1.3S channels.
evidence: This is speculation based on the differences between the current findings and previous work in Xenopus oocytes.

claim: While close proximity is necessary, it is not sufficient to allow channel interactions.
source: Our results suggest that while close proximity is necessary, it is certainly not sufficient to allow channel interactions.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that both CaV1.3S and CaV1.3L form clusters but only CaV1.3S channels couple.

claim: The mechanism allowing neighboring CaV1.3S channels to interact seems to be structural rather than organizational.
source: These results also suggest that the mechanism allowing neighboring CaV1.3S channels to interact seems to be structural rather than organizational.
evidence: This is an inference based on the differential coupling behavior of CaV1.3S and CaV1.3L despite similar clustering.

claim: CaV1.3 channels are generally classified as high-voltage activated channels.
source: Although CaV1.3 channels are generally classified as high-voltage activated channels, their lower activation range allows them to generate subthreshold depolarizations that support repetitive firing (Olson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is established knowledge about CaV1.3 channel classification.

claim: The lower activation range of CaV1.3 channels allows them to generate subthreshold depolarizations that support repetitive firing.
source: Although CaV1.3 channels are generally classified as high-voltage activated channels, their lower activation range allows them to generate subthreshold depolarizations that support repetitive firing (Olson et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Short variants of CaV1.3 are more voltage-sensitive than CaV1.3L channels.
source: This is in particular true for the short variants of CaV1.3, which are more voltage-sensitive than CaV1.3L channels (Bock et al., 2011; Tan et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CaV1.3S channels can coordinate their openings through a physical interaction to facilitate Ca2+ entry at low membrane potentials.
source: Our results reveal a new and striking characteristic of CaV1.3S channels: they can coordinate their openings through a physical interaction to facilitate Ca2+ entry at low membrane potentials.
evidence: This is a summary of the key finding of the study.

claim: CaV1.3 channels are clustered in dendritic spines in hippocampal neurons.
source: In addition, the fact that CaV1.3 channels are clustered in dendritic spines in these neurons (Gao et al., 2006; Jenkins et al., 2010) raises the possibility that their coordinated gating and boosting of Ca2+ entry may have a significant effect on synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The coordinated gating and boosting of Ca2+ entry by CaV1.3 channels may have a significant effect on synaptic plasticity.
source: In addition, the fact that CaV1.3 channels are clustered in dendritic spines in these neurons (Gao et al., 2006; Jenkins et al., 2010) raises the possibility that their coordinated gating and boosting of Ca2+ entry may have a significant effect on synaptic plasticity.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential physiological implications of the findings.

claim: Subthreshold activation of CaV1.3 channels is a key component of pacemaking and oscillatory behavior in neurons in the brain, such as dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra.
source: Subthreshold activation of CaV1.3 channels is also a key component of pacemaking and oscillatory behavior in neurons in the brain, such as dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, the principal neurons affected in Parkinson's disease (Guzman et al., 2009; Puopolo et al., 2007).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Alterations in the cooperative gating of CaV1.3S might contribute to the Ca2+ excitotoxicity observed in multiple pathological conditions, including Parkinson's neurodegeneration.
source: In this context, it is tempting to speculate that alterations in the cooperative gating of CaV1.3S might contribute to the Ca2+ excitotoxicity observed in multiple pathological conditions, including Parkinson's neurodegeneration.
evidence: This is speculation about the potential pathological implications of the findings.

claim: Ca2+-driven physical interactions among clustered CaV1.3S channels lead to cooperative gating of these channels and the enhanced Ca2+ influx that underlies the self-sustained firing of hippocampal neurons.
source: In summary, our data indicate that Ca2+-driven physical interactions among clustered CaV1.3S channels lead to cooperative gating of these channels and the enhanced Ca2+ influx that underlies the self-sustained firing of hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is a summary of the main findings and their functional implications.

claim: Cooperative CaV1.3S channel gating may play an important role in pathological conditions such as Parkinson's disease, spasticity, and memory loss.
source: It is anticipated that future studies may reveal that cooperative CaV1.3S channel gating plays an important role in pathological conditions such as Parkinson's disease, spasticity, and memory loss, as well as in physiological functions as diverse as hearing and the modulation of heart rate, where CaV1.3 channels play a key role.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future findings and broader implications.

claim: Cooperative CaV1.3S channel gating may play an important role in physiological functions as diverse as hearing and the modulation of heart rate.
source: It is anticipated that future studies may reveal that cooperative CaV1.3S channel gating plays an important role in pathological conditions such as Parkinson's disease, spasticity, and memory loss, as well as in physiological functions as diverse as hearing and the modulation of heart rate, where CaV1.3 channels play a key role.
evidence: This is speculation about potential future findings and broader implications.

claim: The findings point to a novel, general mechanism for the dynamic modulation of ionic currents through L-type CaV1.3S and CaV1.2 channels.
source: Finally, our findings point to a novel, general mechanism for the dynamic modulation of ionic currents through L-type CaV1.3S and CaV1.2 channels.
evidence: This is a broader implication of the findings suggesting a general mechanism.

claim: In SA node cells, Ca2+ entry through CaV1.3 and CaV1.2 channels is a key feature in the generation of pacemaker activity.
source: For example, in SA node cells, Ca2+ entry through CaV1.3 and CaV1.2 channels is a key feature in the generation of pacemaker activity (Mangoni et al., 2003; Platzer et al., 2000; Striessnig et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: CaV1.3 channels play a critical role in controlling pacemaker activity in SAN cells through the activation of RyR and the triggering of local Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR).
source: In addition, it has been shown in a recent paper that CaV1.3 channels play a critical role in controlling pacemaker activity in SAN cells through the activation of RyR and the triggering of local Ca2+ release from the sarcoplasmic reticulum (SR) (Torrente et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Spontaneous junctional SR Ca2+ release events could induce multimerization of nearby CaV1.3S, which could produce persistent inward Ca2+ currents that increase the number of RyR activated, thereby driving SA node cells closer to the threshold for action potential generation.
source: The present results suggest a potential new mechanism for Ca2+-dependent control of pacing in these cells. Accordingly, spontaneous junctional SR Ca2+ release events could induce multimerization of nearby CaV1.3S, which, once fused, could produce persistent inward Ca2+ currents that increase the number of RyR activated, thereby driving SA node cells closer to the threshold for action potential generation.
evidence: This is speculation about a potential mechanism in SA node cells based on the current findings.
